title: How to Make Good Work Happen Over and Over
author: Greg McKeown
summary: In this 1-Minute Wednesday, Greg McKeown argues that great work deserves more than a reflexive 'great job.' Effective praise carries details because details signal that someone was paying attention, and leaders who move quickly often skip the useful part of saying what they saw and why it mattered. He offers a two-sentence formula: when you did X, it created Y, and that mattered because Z. To support the claim he cites a small randomized study in which medical students given general compliments rated the experience as more satisfying yet did not improve their surgical knot-tying scores, while those given specific feedback did. His takeaway is that an interaction can feel good without giving a person anything to build on, so to replicate good behavior leaders must be explicit about it. The piece ends with a simple prompt to pause before saying 'great job' and name what exactly mattered.
points: Praise that names the specific behavior carries more weight because it shows the leader was paying attention.
The formula 'When you [did X], it created [Y]. That mattered because [Z]' combines appreciation with useful information in two sentences.
In the cited knot-tying study, general compliments felt better but produced no significant improvement, while specific feedback improved scores.
Leaders under time pressure default to 'great job,' so the habit needs a deliberate pause to counter it.
To replicate a behavior, a leader has to be explicit about it and about the difference it made.

For example: "When you asked her if there was more, she surfaced a risk we had missed. That mattered because it changed our decision before we committed.
